questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) With the aid of diagrams, describe and account for the formation of each of the following:

(i) Horst; (4 marks)

(ii) Boudinage. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Horst (4 marks).**

A **horst** is a **block of crust that stands higher than the blocks on both sides**; it is **bounded by two normal faults that dip (hade) away from the block**.

- **Formation:** **tensional (extensional) forces** pull the crust apart, so the crust is stretched. Two roughly parallel **normal faults** develop; the blocks **outside** the faults slide down along them (they form downthrown **grabens** or rift valleys) while the **central block remains high** (or is relatively uplifted). The result is a **raised, flat-topped or tilted block with steep fault scarps**. Faults dip away from the horst.
- **Examples:** the Black Forest and Vosges (on the flanks of the Rhine rift valley), and horst blocks in the East African Rift system.
- *Sketch to draw:* a cross-section with a raised central block between two normal faults that slope outwards, arrows showing the tension (pulling apart) and the movement down on both sides, and the labels horst, graben, fault plane, hade, downthrow, scarp.

**(ii) Boudinage (4 marks).**

**Boudinage** is the structure in which a **competent (strong, brittle) layer** such as sandstone, limestone or a dolerite sheet, **between weaker (incompetent) layers** such as shale or schist, is **stretched and pulled apart into sausage-like or lens-like bodies (boudins)**. The boudins are separated by narrow gaps or by **necks (pinch-and-swell)**, which are filled by the flowing incompetent material or by quartz or calcite veins.

- **Formation:** it happens when the rock is **extended (stretched) parallel to the layering**, or flattened at right angles to it, under **ductile conditions (deep, high temperature, such as in folded and metamorphic belts)**. The competent layer is much less able to deform (it has **a high viscosity contrast** with the surrounding rock), so it **necks and breaks**, while the weak rock flows into the gaps. The long axes of the boudins are **perpendicular to the direction of extension**.
- *Sketch to draw:* a cross-section with a strong layer broken into separated, rounded or rectangular boudins in a darker weak matrix, with arrows showing the stretching direction, and the gaps filled by quartz.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Distinguish between each of the following:

(i) Dip and strike; (3 marks)

(ii) Fault breccias and fault gouge. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Dip and strike (3 marks).**

- **Strike** is the **direction (compass bearing) of a horizontal line drawn on an inclined bed or fault plane**, that is, the line along which the plane meets a horizontal surface (for example N 30° E).
- **Dip** is the **maximum angle at which the bed or plane is inclined from the horizontal**, measured **at right angles to the strike** (in the direction of steepest slope), with the direction (for example $25^\circ$ toward the south-east). The dip is **perpendicular to the strike**. Both are measured with a **clinometer compass** and shown on maps by a T-shaped symbol with the dip value.

**(ii) Fault breccias and fault gouge (2 marks).**

- **Fault breccia:** **coarse, angular fragments** of the broken wall rock produced by **crushing along a fault**; the fragments are visible (larger than about 2 mm) and may be held together by cement such as calcite or quartz.
- **Fault gouge:** a **very fine-grained, soft, clay-like (powdered) material** formed by **intense grinding** of the rock along the fault; the grains are too small to see, the material is **not cemented (incohesive)** and it is often impermeable.
